```{r setup, include=FALSE}

# SETUP: DEFAULT BEHAVIORS FOR CODE CHUNKS
# *****************************************************************************
# These settings control how R code chunks behave in your report:
# - echo = FALSE: Don't show the code, just the output
# - message = FALSE: Suppress package loading messages
# - warning = FALSE: Suppress warning messages
# - dpi = 300: High resolution for all plots (publication quality)
# - fig.width/fig.height: Default dimensions for plots in inches
# - dev = 'png': Use PNG device for better font rendering in HTML output
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  dpi = 300,
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 5,
  dev = 'png'
)

# KNOLOGY COLOR PALETTE
# *****************************************************************************
# Use these color variables throughout your report for consistent branding.
# They can be used in ggplot2 with: geom_point(color = kBlue)
# Or with scale_fill_manual(values = c(kAqua, kOrange, kPurple))

# Primary Knology colors
kBlue   <-  "#266093"         # Trusted Blue (primary brand color)
kSky    <-  "#7D9BC0"         # Horizon Blue (light accent)
kYellow <-  "#D8C827"         # Optimistic Citrine (highlight)
kOrange <-  "#F36C3E"         # Radiant Coral (accent)
kGreen  <-  "#6CA443"         # New Leaf (nature/growth)
kAqua   <-  "#00A2AE"         # Ocean (behaviors)
kPurple <-  "#943A80"         # Passion (culture)
kText   <-  "#002F6C"         # Dark Blue (Headers)
kBlack  <-  "#101820"         # Black (Body text)
axis.col<-  "#cccccc"         # Light grey for axes

# Color vector for multi-category plots (use this for 6+ categories)
# Order: Aqua → Orange → Purple → Yellow → Green → Blue
Knology.bar.col <- c(kAqua, kOrange, kPurple, kYellow, kGreen, kBlue)

# Recycles the Knology palette to however many groups exist
knology_pal <- function(n) rep(Knology.bar.col, length.out = n)

# LOAD FONTS
# *****************************************************************************
# Ubuntu is used for headers and plot text
# Open Sans is used for body text (via CSS)
# showtext_auto() enables custom fonts in plots
# showtext_opts() sets the DPI for proper rendering in HTML/PNG output
sysfonts::font_add_google("Ubuntu")
sysfonts::font_add_google("Open Sans")
showtext::showtext_auto()
showtext::showtext_opts(dpi = 300)  # Match the DPI setting for proper text scaling

# LOAD REQUIRED PACKAGES
# *****************************************************************************
library(ggpubr)       # Publication-ready plots and statistical comparisons
library(tidyverse)    # Data manipulation and visualization (includes ggplot2, dplyr, etc.)
library(kableExtra)
library(readxl)

# SET SEED FOR REPRODUCIBILITY
# *****************************************************************************
# This ensures that any random operations (sampling, simulations) 
# produce the same results each time you knit the document
set.seed(1234)

# DEFINE KNOLOGY GRAPH STYLE
# *****************************************************************************
# This theme removes unnecessary chart elements and applies Knology branding
# Use it by adding "+ graphStyle" to any ggplot
graphStyle <- theme_bw() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "Ubuntu", size = 18),         # Use Ubuntu font, size 18 for all text
    panel.border = element_blank(),                            # Remove border around plot
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),                        # Remove major gridlines
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),                        # Remove minor gridlines
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),  # Transparent panel
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA),    # Transparent background
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent"),    # Transparent legend
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 18),                     # X-axis labels size
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 18),                     # Y-axis labels size
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 18, margin = margin(10, 0, 0, 0)), # X-axis title
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 18),                    # Y-axis title
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, hjust = 0.5, color = kText), # Plot title (centered, larger)
    legend.text = element_text(size = 16),                     # Legend text
    legend.title = element_text(size = 18)                     # Legend title
  )

# WRAP LONG AXIS LABELS
# *****************************************************************************
# Wraps labels to a new line after a specified character limit
# Usage: scale_x_discrete(labels = wrap_labels(20))
# Adjust width = number to control where the line breaks

wrap_labels <- function(width = 15) {
  function(x) stringr::str_wrap(x, width = width)
}
```

```{r data-preparation}

# ***** PROJECT-SPECIFIC CONFIGURATION ****************************************
# EDIT THIS SECTION FOR EACH PROJECT.
# All the choices that vary project-to-project are gathered here so you only
# have to look in one place when adapting the template.

# 1. GROUPING VARIABLE
#    The column used to split tables and color plots (e.g. "Species", "Game",
#    "Condition", "Site"). Must exist in mydata after any renaming below.
group_var <- "Species"

# 2. NUMERIC VARIABLES FOR DESCRIPTIVE STATS TABLE AND PLOTS
#    List the column names you want summarised. These will appear as rows
#    in the descriptive stats table and as the y-axis in plots.
numeric_vars <- c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width", "Petal.Length", "Petal.Width")

# 3. CATEGORICAL VARIABLES FOR FREQUENCY TABLES
#    List the column names you want one-table-per-variable frequency output for.
#    Remove any free-text or ID columns
cat_vars <- c("Species")

# 4. LIKERT LEVELS (ordered low → high)
#    If your data has Likert-scale responses, define the correct order here so
#    tables and plots sort properly. Delete this block if not applicable.
likert_levels <- c(
  "Disagree Strongly",
  "Disagree Moderately",
  "Disagree Slightly",
  "Agree Slightly",
  "Agree Moderately",
  "Agree Strongly"
)

# 5. COLUMNS TO APPLY LIKERT FACTOR ORDERING
#    List any columns that use the likert_levels scale defined above.
#    Delete this block if not applicable.
likert_cols <- c()   # e.g. c("Setup_Ease", "Learning", "Parent_Response")

# ******* WIDE-TO-LONG PIVOT (ONLY NEEDED FOR REPEATED-BLOCK SURVEY DATA) *************
# Skip this section entirely if your data is already in long format or has
# no repeated question blocks (e.g. the same questions asked once per condition).
#
# When to use it: your data has columns like "Question 1", "Question 2",
# "Question 3" — the same questions repeated for different conditions/groups,
# distinguished only by a numeric suffix.
#
# HOW IT WORKS:
#   pivot_longer with names_pattern splits each column name into two parts:
#   (1) the base question stem  →  becomes the new column name
#   (2) the suffix number       →  becomes the grouping variable
#
# INSTRUCTIONS:
#   a. Set repeated_question_stems to the exact base question texts (without
#      the trailing number).
#   b. Set group_labels to map each suffix number to its human-readable name.
#   c. Set repeated_group_var to what you want to call the grouping column
#      (e.g. "Game", "Condition", "Visit").
#   d. Rename the resulting columns to short clean names in the rename() call.
#   e. Update numeric_vars and cat_vars above to use the new short names.
#   f. Replace mydata with mydata_long in all plots and tables below.

# ***UNCOMMENT AND FILL IN IF YOUR DATA NEEDS A PIVOT ***

# repeated_question_stems <- c(
#   "Question stem one",       # exact text, no trailing number
#   "Question stem two",
#   "Question stem three"
# )
#
# group_labels <- c(
#   "1" = "Group Name 1",      # suffix -> human-readable label
#   "2" = "Group Name 2",
#   "3" = "Group Name 3"
# )
#
# repeated_group_var <- "Group"   # what to call the new grouping column
#
# pivot_regex <- str_c(
#   "^(", str_c(repeated_question_stems, collapse = "|"), ") ([0-9]+)$"
# )
#
# mydata_long <- mydata %>%
#   pivot_longer(
#     cols         = matches(pivot_regex),
#     names_to     = c(".value", "suffix"),
#     names_pattern = pivot_regex
#   ) %>%
#   mutate(
#     !!repeated_group_var := factor(group_labels[suffix], levels = group_labels)
#   ) %>%
#   rename(
#     ShortName1 = `Question stem one`,    # give each question a short clean name
#     ShortName2 = `Question stem two`,
#     ShortName3 = `Question stem three`
#   )

# ************ STANDARD CLEANING*******************************
# Converts empty strings and non-breaking spaces (common in survey exports)
# to true NA, and trims any accidental whitespace.

mydata <- mydata %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), str_trim)) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~na_if(., ""))) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~na_if(., "\u00a0")))

# Survey exports from Excel often store numeric columns as character when any
# cell contains a non-numeric value (like a non-breaking space or stray text).
# suppressWarnings() silences the "NAs introduced by coercion" message, which
# is expected — those were already non-numeric and are correctly becoming NA.

#mydata <- mydata %>%
  #mutate(across(all_of(numeric_vars), ~suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.))))

# Apply ordered Likert factor if likert_cols is populated
if (length(likert_cols) > 0) {
  mydata <- mydata %>%
    mutate(across(all_of(likert_cols),
                  ~factor(., levels = likert_levels, ordered = TRUE)))
}

# Rename the grouping variable to a standard internal name so all downstream
# code works without modification when you change group_var above.
mydata <- mydata %>%
  rename(Group = all_of(group_var))

# Remap cat_vars: if the grouping column was listed there, update it to "Group"
# so downstream walk() finds the column under its new internal name.
cat_vars <- str_replace(cat_vars, fixed(group_var), "Group")
```

## Results

### Descriptive Statistics

```{r descriptive-stats, results='asis'}

# Detect output format
is_word <- isTRUE(knitr::opts_knit$get("rmarkdown.pandoc.to") == "docx")

# HELPER: RENDER ONE KABLE TABLE
# *****************************************************************************
# Centralises the is_word switch so it doesn't repeat inside every walk() call.
# Pass it any data frame + caption and it renders correctly for HTML or Word.
render_table <- function(tbl, caption, col_names = colnames(tbl),
                         align = NULL, collapse_col = NULL) {

  k <- knitr::kable(tbl, caption = caption,
                    col.names = col_names,
                    align = align)
  if (!is_word) {
    k <- k %>%
      kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                    full_width = FALSE)
    if (!is.null(collapse_col)) {
      k <- k %>% collapse_rows(columns = collapse_col, valign = "top")
    }
  }
  print(k)
}

# FREQUENCY TABLE FOR CATEGORICAL ITEMS
# *****************************************************************************
# NA rows are dropped before counting.
# Valid N reflects only rows with a response — this matches the N used in means.

# walk() iterates over cat_vars and prints a separate table for each one.
# Unlike lapply, walk() is designed for side effects (like printing) rather
# than collecting results — it's the tidyverse tool for "do this for each item".
# results='asis' on the chunk header is required so knitr renders the HTML
# tables instead of printing them as raw text.

walk(cat_vars, function(col) {

  tbl <- mydata %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[col]])) %>%
    group_by(Response = as.character(.data[[col]])) %>%
    summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(
      Valid_N = sum(n),
      Pct     = round(n / Valid_N * 100, 1)
    ) %>%
    select(Response, n, Pct, Valid_N)

  render_table(
    tbl,
    caption   = str_c("Response frequencies for: ", col),
    col_names = c("Response", "n", "%", "Valid N"),
    align     = "lrrr"
  )
})


# DESCRIPTIVE STATISTICS TABLE
# *****************************************************************************
# group_by(Group) produces one block of statistics per group level.
# summarise(across(...)) applies all 6 stat functions to every numeric variable
# in one step.
# pivot_longer then reshapes to tidy format: each row = one group × one variable.
#
# To remove grouping and get overall statistics, delete the group_by(Group) line
# and replace -Group with everything() in pivot_longer.

desc_table <- mydata %>%
  group_by(Group) %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      all_of(numeric_vars),
      list(
        N      = ~sum(!is.na(.)),
        Mean   = ~round(mean(., na.rm = TRUE), 2),
        SD     = ~round(sd(.,   na.rm = TRUE), 2),
        Median = ~round(median(., na.rm = TRUE), 2),
        Min    = ~round(min(.,  na.rm = TRUE), 2),
        Max    = ~round(max(.,  na.rm = TRUE), 2)
      ),
      .names = "{.col}__{.fn}"   # double underscore = reliable split point for pivot_longer
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = -Group,
    names_to  = c("Variable", ".value"),   # split col name into Variable + stat name
    names_sep = "__"
  ) %>%
  select(Group, Variable, N, Mean, SD, Median, Min, Max)

render_table(
  desc_table,
  caption     = "Descriptive statistics by group.",
  col_names   = c("Group", "Variable", "N", "Mean", "SD", "Median", "Min", "Max"),
  align       = "llrrrrrr",
  collapse_col = 1
)
```

### Distribution by Group

```{r violin-plot, fig.cap="Figure 1. Distribution of the primary outcome variable by group."}

# VIOLIN PLOT
# *****************************************************************************
# UPDATE: Change y = to your primary numeric variable of interest.

ggplot(mydata, aes(x = Group, y = .data[[numeric_vars[1]]], fill = Group)) +
  geom_violin(trim = FALSE, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, fill = "white", outlier.shape = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = knology_pal(n_distinct(mydata$Group))) +
  labs(
    title = str_c("Distribution of ", numeric_vars[1], " by Group"),
    x = "",
    y = numeric_vars[1]
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = wrap_labels(12)) +
  graphStyle +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Mean Comparison

```{r bar-plot, fig.cap="Figure 2. Mean values by group with standard error bars."}

# BAR PLOT WITH ERROR BARS
# *****************************************************************************
# UPDATE: Change the variable inside mean() and sd() to your outcome of interest.

bar_data <- mydata %>%
  group_by(Group) %>%
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(.data[[numeric_vars[1]]], na.rm = TRUE),
    SE   = sd(.data[[numeric_vars[1]]],   na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.nan(Mean))    # add this line

ggplot(bar_data, aes(x = Group, y = Mean, fill = Group)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = Mean - SE, ymax = Mean + SE),
    width = 0.2,
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = knology_pal(n_distinct(bar_data$Group))) +
  labs(
    title = str_c("Mean ", numeric_vars[1], " by Group"),
    x = "",
    y = str_c("Mean ", numeric_vars[1])
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = wrap_labels(12)) +
  graphStyle +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Means with Confidence Intervals

```{r means-plot, fig.cap="Figure 4. Mean values with 95% confidence intervals by group."}

# HORIZONTAL MEANS PLOT
# *****************************************************************************
means_data <- mydata %>%
  group_by(Group) %>%
  summarise(
    Mean  = mean(.data[[numeric_vars[1]]], na.rm = TRUE),
    Lower = Mean - 1.96 * sd(.data[[numeric_vars[1]]], na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    Upper = Mean + 1.96 * sd(.data[[numeric_vars[1]]], na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.nan(Mean)) %>%                  # drop groups with no valid data
  mutate(Group = fct_reorder(Group, Mean))

ggplot(means_data, aes(x = Mean, y = Group)) +
  geom_errorbarh(
    aes(xmin = Lower, xmax = Upper),
    height = 0.2,
    linewidth = 1,
    color = kBlue
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 4, color = kBlue) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = str_c("Mean ", numeric_vars[1])) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = "", labels = wrap_labels(20)) +
  labs(title = str_c("Mean ", numeric_vars[1], " by Group (95% CI)")) +
  graphStyle +
  theme(axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

### Multi-Variable Comparison

```{r grouped-means, fig.cap="Figure 5. Mean values across all numeric variables and groups."}

# GROUPED HORIZONTAL MEANS PLOT
# *****************************************************************************
# Compares all numeric_vars side by side, colored by Group.
# Useful for showing a profile across multiple outcomes at once.

grouped_data <- mydata %>%
  group_by(Group) %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      all_of(numeric_vars),
      ~mean(., na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = -Group,
    names_to  = "Variable",
    values_to = "Mean"
  ) %>%
  mutate(Variable = fct_reorder(Variable, Mean, .fun = mean))

ggplot(grouped_data, aes(x = Mean, y = Variable, color = Group)) +
  geom_point(
    size = 3,
    position = position_dodge(-0.5)
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = knology_pal(n_distinct(grouped_data$Group))) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Mean Value") +
  scale_y_discrete(name = "", labels = wrap_labels(25)) +
  labs(title = "Mean Values Across Variables and Groups") +
  graphStyle +
  theme(
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "right",
    plot.margin = margin(r = 0.75, t = 0.25, unit = "lines")
  )
```
